title: Replication, backups, failover and pooling
scopeHtml: Scope: streaming and logical replication, lag, backups, PITR, failover, PgBouncer connection pooling.

notes.title: Why replicate
notes.html:
Replication keeps copies of the database on other machines. Three separate reasons, each with different requirements:

  1. High availability: if the primary dies, a copy takes over.
  2. Read scaling: send read-only queries to replicas.
  3. Backup and analytics isolation: run heavy reports on a copy so they do not slow production.

Single-writer model (Postgres default): one primary accepts writes; replicas are read-only copies that continuously apply the primary's changes. Multi-writer is a different, much harder world (file 11).

Worked example. A product has 2,000 reads/s and 100 writes/s. A single primary handles both, but peak reads reach 8,000/s. Add 2 replicas and route reads: each replica serves ~4,000/s; primary stays at 100 writes/s plus WAL shipping. Cost is a few extra instances; the risk is stale reads (replica lag).

Industry examples. Instagram and GitHub ran large primary-plus-replicas fleets for years. Most managed Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora) offers one-click read replicas.

Everyday analogy. A master recipe book and photocopies in each kitchen: copies are updated after the master, so a copy can be a page behind.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming replicas help write throughput. They do not.
  • Forgetting that every replica must replay all writes, so replica CPU/IO must handle the write rate.

notes.title: Streaming (physical) replication
notes.html:
Physical streaming replication ships the primary's WAL records over TCP to standbys, which replay them byte for byte. The standby is an exact binary copy: same version, same architecture, whole cluster (all databases).

Setup essentials:

# primary postgresql.conf
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 10
max_replication_slots = 10
hot_standby = on            # standby allows read-only queries
# standby bootstrap
pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D /var/lib/postgresql/16/main \
  -R -X stream --slot=replica1
# -R writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo for you

Replication slots make the primary keep WAL until the standby has received it, so a lagging or disconnected standby does not lose its place. Danger: an abandoned slot makes WAL pile up until the disk fills (use max_slot_wal_keep_size).

Synchronous vs asynchronous.

  • Async (default): COMMIT returns after the local WAL flush; a replica may miss the last transactions if the primary dies (small data loss: RPO > 0).
  • Sync: synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (replica1, replica2)'; COMMIT also waits for a standby; RPO = 0 but commit latency now includes a network round trip (~1 to 2 ms in one region, 50 ms+ cross-region), and if all sync standbys are down, writes block.

Measuring lag:

-- on primary
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Decision gravity. Sync vs async is an availability-vs-durability dial and reversible via config. Choosing a quorum like ANY 1 (a,b) keeps writes going if one standby dies.

Everyday analogy. A court stenographer sending live transcripts to a second office. Sync means the judge waits for the second office to confirm each line.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing sync replication means reads from the replica are always fresh (replay can still lag: remote_apply solves that).
  • Leaving a dead replication slot.
  • Confusing physical (binary, same major version) with logical replication.

notes.title: Replica lag and read-your-writes
notes.html:
Replica lag is the delay between a commit on the primary and its visibility on a replica. Normally milliseconds; under load, long queries on the replica, or network trouble it can reach seconds or minutes.

Symptom the user sees: "I posted a comment, refreshed, and it is gone." (stale read). Fixes (read-your-writes):

  1. Read from the primary for a short time (e.g. 5 s) after the user writes (session flag or cookie).
  2. Pass the LSN: after a write, read pg_current_wal_lsn(); route the following read to a replica only when pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN.
  3. Use synchronous_commit = remote_apply for critical flows.
  4. Make the UI optimistic (show the new comment locally).

Replica conflicts. A long query on a replica can clash with WAL replay that removes rows the query still needs. Postgres either cancels the query (max_standby_streaming_delay, default 30 s) or delays replay. hot_standby_feedback = on tells the primary to keep those rows, at the cost of primary bloat.

Worked example. A nightly report runs 40 minutes on replica 2. With default settings, replay pauses up to 30 s and then the query is cancelled with "canceling statement due to conflict with recovery". Options: a dedicated reporting replica with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 (unbounded, lag grows) and no user traffic.

Industry examples. Facebook-style systems tag requests with write timestamps/LSNs; Rails has automatic multi-database role switching with a "delay after write" window.

Everyday analogy. Posting a letter and immediately asking the neighbour whether it has arrived.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending all reads to replicas without addressing stale reads after writes.
  • Not monitoring lag (replay_lag) or alerting on it.

notes.title: Logical replication
notes.html:
Logical replication ships row-level changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) decoded from the WAL, per table, using publish/subscribe. Unlike physical replication, the target can be a different major version, a subset of tables, or even a different system.

-- publisher
CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders, customers;
-- subscriber
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION app_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=old dbname=app user=repl'
  PUBLICATION app_pub;

Needs wal_level = logical. Caveats: tables need a primary key (or replica identity); DDL and sequences are not replicated automatically; large transactions are slow to apply.

Uses:

  • Zero-downtime major upgrades: subscribe a new-version server, let it catch up, then switch the app.
  • CDC: Debezium reads the logical decoding stream and publishes to Kafka.
  • Selective copies: feed an analytics database.

Industry examples. Many companies upgrade Postgres 12 to 16 using logical replication with a few seconds of cutover. Shopify and others use CDC streams to build search indexes and caches.

Decision gravity. Physical for HA and read scaling (simple, complete); logical for upgrades, partial replication and event streams. Logical slots, like physical ones, retain WAL if the consumer stalls.

Everyday analogy. Physical is photocopying the whole book page by page; logical is sending a list of "change line 4 to X" edits for chosen chapters.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming logical replication copies schema changes.
  • Using logical replication for failover without handling sequences.

notes.title: Backups: logical and physical
notes.html:
A backup you have never restored is not a backup. Two families:

Logical (pg_dump) Physical (pg_basebackup, snapshots)
Output SQL or custom-format dump of objects Copy of data files plus WAL
Restore speed Slow (re-inserts, rebuilds indexes) Fast (copy back, replay WAL)
Cross-version Yes No (same major)
Granularity One table or schema possible Whole cluster
PITR No Yes with WAL archive 
# logical, parallel, custom format
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -f /backups/app_2026-11-09 appdb
pg_restore -j 4 -d appdb_restored /backups/app_2026-11-09

# physical base backup
pg_basebackup -D /backups/base -Ft -z -X stream -P

Worked example. 1 TB database: pg_dump + restore takes hours (rebuilding indexes dominates); a physical base backup copies at, say, 200 MB/s, about 1.5 hours, and restore is the same plus WAL replay. A cloud volume snapshot is near instant to create (copy-on-write) but you must handle consistency (Postgres crash-consistent snapshot plus WAL is usually safe; confirm with your provider's docs).

Rules (the 3-2-1 idea). 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 off-site/off-account. Encrypt backups, test restores on a schedule, and protect backups from the same ransomware or accidental-delete path as production.

Tools. pgBackRest, Barman, WAL-G handle base backups, WAL archiving, retention, compression, encryption and parallel restore to S3/GCS.

Everyday analogy. A fire drill: owning an extinguisher is not enough, you need to have practised using it.

Common interview traps.

  • Never testing restores.
  • Keeping backups on the same disk or account as the database.
  • Believing replicas are backups (a bad DELETE replicates instantly).

notes.title: Point-in-time recovery (PITR)
notes.html:
PITR restores the database to any moment (for example 10:41:59, just before a bad DELETE) by restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a target.

Setup:

# postgresql.conf on primary
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'

Recovery:

# on the restored host, then create recovery.signal
restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-get %f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-09 10:41:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

Metrics: RPO (how much data you can lose) is bounded by WAL archive frequency (or zero with streaming plus sync standby). RTO (how long recovery takes) = restore time + replay time. For 1 TB with weekly full + daily incremental backups and 20 MB/s WAL, RTO is perhaps 1 to 3 hours (illustrative); shortening it means more frequent base backups or a warm standby.

Worked example (incident). At 10:42 an engineer runs DELETE FROM orders without WHERE. Steps: stop writes to prevent more damage, restore the latest base backup onto a NEW server, replay WAL to 10:41:59, then dump the missing rows from the recovered copy and re-insert into production (or swap). Time: ~2 hours, and all other writes after 10:42 on prod are preserved if you copy rows instead of swapping.

Industry examples. GitLab's 2017 database incident (public postmortem) is the canonical lesson: five backup methods, none working when needed. Managed services expose "restore to point in time" built on exactly this.

Decision gravity. Retention (7 vs 35 days) is a cost-vs-safety dial and easy to change; archiving WAL must be enabled before you need it, since you cannot recover to a moment that was not archived.

Everyday analogy. A video recording with save points: rewind to the last save, then fast-forward to just before the mistake.

Common interview traps.

  • No WAL archiving, so only restore-to-backup-time is possible.
  • Replaying to a time after the damage.
  • Forgetting RTO includes validation and cutover, not just restore.

notes.title: Failover and high availability
notes.html:
Failover is promoting a standby to primary when the primary fails, then redirecting clients. Manual failover takes minutes and mistakes; automated tools do it in about 10 to 30 s.

Pieces:

  1. Failure detection (missed heartbeats, usually a few seconds to avoid false triggers).
  2. Leader election with a consensus store (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper) so only ONE node becomes primary. Without it you get split brain: two primaries accepting writes and diverging data.
  3. Promotion (pg_promote()), then other standbys follow the new primary (pg_rewind can fix the old primary to rejoin).
  4. Client routing: virtual IP, DNS with short TTL, HAProxy/PgBouncer, or a managed endpoint.
  5. Fencing: make sure the old primary cannot take writes (STONITH: shut the node down, remove its network).

Tools: Patroni (etcd-based, the de facto standard for self-managed), repmgr, Stolon; managed services (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora, Cloud SQL HA) hide all this.

Worked example. Primary dies at 12:00:00. etcd leader key TTL 30 s, loop_wait 10 s, retry_timeout 10 s. At about 12:00:30 a standby (most up-to-date, sync) grabs the key, promotes in ~1 s, HAProxy health checks switch in ~5 s. Total about 35 s of unavailability; with async replication up to the lag worth of commits may be lost. RTO ~35 s; RPO depends on sync mode.

Incident pattern. False failover: a network blip makes the primary look dead, a standby promotes, the old primary is alive and still receiving some clients: split brain. Prevent with fencing, a quorum store and a lease that the old primary must renew to keep serving.

Decision gravity. Automatic failover is a trade: faster recovery vs risk of wrong promotion. Choose thresholds with data. Cross-region failover is a bigger one-way operational decision (DNS, data loss window, client config).

Everyday analogy. A captain going overboard: the crew must agree on exactly one new captain, and the old captain must not keep issuing orders from the water.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing failover without fencing or consensus.
  • Saying failover is zero downtime. It is seconds to tens of seconds.
  • Ignoring that apps must reconnect and retry.

notes.title: Connection pooling
notes.html:
Every Postgres connection is an OS process (about 5 to 10 MB baseline, more with work_mem usage), so thousands of connections hurt. Practical sweet spot: roughly 2 to 4 active connections per CPU core. A pooler multiplexes many client connections over a small set of server connections.

PgBouncer modes:

  • Session: a server connection is held for the whole client session. Safest, least multiplexing.
  • Transaction: server connection held only during a transaction. Best multiplexing (the usual choice) but breaks session state: session-level advisory locks, SET without LOCAL, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and (historically) protocol-level prepared statements. Check your PgBouncer version for prepared-statement support.
  • Statement: one statement at a time; rarely usable.
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
app = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=app

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40        ; server connections per db/user pair
reserve_pool_size = 5
server_idle_timeout = 600

Worked example. 100 app pods x 20 pool connections = 2,000 connections hitting a 16-core Postgres: context switching, memory, and max_connections limits. Put PgBouncer in front with default_pool_size = 40: 2,000 client connections share 40 server connections, CPU drops, latency improves. Also size app-side pools small (e.g. HikariCP maximumPoolSize 10) since a large app pool does not make the database faster.

Incident pattern. Deploy restarts 100 pods; each opens connections at once: "too many clients already" or a connection storm. Metric: pg_stat_activity count versus max_connections; mitigate with a pooler, slow starts and max_connections headroom.

Industry examples. Supabase, Heroku, and many SaaS vendors run PgBouncer or Odyssey/pgcat in front of Postgres; AWS RDS Proxy is the managed analogue.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with 10 waiters for 200 diners: you do not hire one waiter per diner.

Common interview traps.

  • Raising max_connections to 5,000 instead of pooling.
  • Using session-level features through a transaction-mode pooler.
  • Forgetting the pooler is itself a component to make highly available.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Replication serves availability, read scaling and isolation; Postgres is single-writer; replicas do not raise write throughput.
  • Physical streaming replication ships WAL; async risks losing recent commits, sync costs a network round trip and can block writes.
  • Replica lag causes stale reads; solve with read-your-writes routing, LSN checks, or remote_apply for critical paths.
  • Logical replication (publish/subscribe, CDC) enables major upgrades and selective copies but does not copy DDL.
  • Backups: logical (portable, slow) vs physical (fast, PITR capable). Use pgBackRest/Barman/WAL-G, 3-2-1, and test restores.
  • PITR = base backup + archived WAL to a target time; define RPO and RTO.
  • Failover needs failure detection, a consensus store, promotion, client routing and fencing to avoid split brain.
  • Pool connections (PgBouncer transaction mode) and keep active connections near 2 to 4 per core.

questions.promptHtml: We have a Postgres primary. Why would you add replicas, and what will replicas not fix?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates say "replicas make the database faster". The signal is knowing the three distinct goals and that writes do not scale.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I add replicas for three reasons: high availability so a copy can take over, read scaling by sending read-only queries to copies, and isolation so reports and backups do not hurt production. They do not raise write throughput, because in Postgres only one primary accepts writes and every replica must replay all of them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Postgres is single-writer. The primary writes WAL; each replica receives the WAL stream and replays it. So the replica's CPU and IO must keep up with the full write rate, not a fraction of it.

App writes -> Primary --WAL--> Replica 1 (reads)
                       --WAL--> Replica 2 (reports)

Each goal has different requirements. HA wants a replica that is close behind (ideally synchronous) and failover tooling. Read scaling tolerates lag but needs routing logic in the app. Analytics isolation wants a replica that may lag a lot but never gets cancelled queries.

Worked numbers: 8,000 reads/s peak, 100 writes/s. Two replicas serve about 4,000 reads/s each; the primary keeps 100 writes/s plus the cost of shipping WAL. The price: stale reads (replica lag) and more instances.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting write throughput to grow with replicas.
  • Forgetting replica hardware must handle the full write rate.
  • Treating a replica as a backup (a bad DELETE replicates instantly).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Would replicas help if the bottleneck is writes? -> No; you need a faster primary, batching, partitioning, or sharding.
  2. Is a replica a backup? -> No, it copies mistakes in milliseconds; you need base backups plus WAL archive.
  3. What breaks when you route reads to replicas? -> Read-your-writes: a user writes then reads a stale copy, so you need routing rules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists "read scaling and failover". The senior answer separates the three goals, names the write ceiling, and mentions lag handling and that replica IO must absorb the full write stream.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams add a fourth replica to fix slow writes, see no improvement, and then discover the primary was the bottleneck all along.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous streaming replication in Postgres, and what does each cost you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can reason about the durability versus latency/availability dial with real numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In async, COMMIT returns after the primary flushes its own WAL; if the primary dies, the last few commits may not have reached a standby, so RPO is above zero. In sync, COMMIT also waits for a standby, so RPO is zero but every commit pays a network round trip, and if the sync standbys are all down, writes block.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Physical replication ships WAL records over TCP to a WAL receiver, which writes then replays them. Where COMMIT waits depends on synchronous_commit:

off / local   : own flush only
remote_write  : standby received and wrote WAL to OS
on            : standby flushed WAL to disk (default for sync standbys)
remote_apply  : standby replayed it, so reads there see the commit

Configuring it:

-- postgresql.conf
-- synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica1, replica2)'
SHOW synchronous_commit;
SELECT application_name, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;

Cost: about 1 to 2 ms extra per commit inside a region, 50 ms+ cross-region. Quorum form ANY 1 (a,b) lets writes continue when one standby dies. FIRST 1 (a,b) prefers priority order.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking sync means replica reads are fresh; only remote_apply gives that.
  • A single sync standby with no fallback: its failure freezes all writes.
  • Cross-region sync replication on a latency-sensitive write path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does RPO mean here? -> The amount of acknowledged data you can lose; async: roughly the replication lag, sync: zero.
  2. How do you stop one dead standby blocking commits? -> Use a quorum with at least two candidates.
  3. Can you pick per transaction? -> Yes, SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off for low-value writes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sync is safer, async is faster". Senior: quantifies the round trip, uses quorum, knows remote_apply, and can decide per-transaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled sync to a standby in another region and p99 write latency jumped from 4 ms to 70 ms overnight.

questions.promptHtml: Physical streaming replication and logical replication both copy data between Postgres servers. When do you use which?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Confusing the two is a common trap; the answer decides upgrade and CDC strategy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Physical replication ships WAL byte for byte, so the standby is an exact binary copy of the whole cluster on the same major version. That is what I use for HA and read replicas. Logical replication ships decoded row changes per table through publish/subscribe, so it can cross major versions, replicate a subset, and feed CDC like Debezium, but it does not copy DDL or sequences.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Logical decoding reads the WAL (needs wal_level = logical) and turns it into INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE per row.

-- publisher
CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders, customers;
-- subscriber
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION app_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=old dbname=app user=repl'
  PUBLICATION app_pub;
Physical Logical
Unit WAL bytes, whole cluster Row changes, chosen tables
Versions Same major Can differ
Target writable No Yes
DDL Replayed (it is WAL) Not replicated
Needs PK No Yes (replica identity)

Both kinds of slots retain WAL if the consumer stalls.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming schema changes flow through logical replication.
  • Forgetting sequences are not synced, so IDs collide after cutover.
  • Tables without a primary key cannot replicate UPDATE/DELETE without replica identity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do a zero-downtime major upgrade? -> Logical-replicate to a new-version server, let it catch up, fix sequences, switch app.
  2. Why can't you use physical across versions? -> The WAL format and catalog layout change per major version.
  3. What happens if a subscriber stalls? -> The slot holds WAL on the publisher until disk fills unless capped.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "logical is per table". The senior adds the DDL/sequence/PK caveats and the slot disk risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Upgrade cutovers have gone wrong because sequences on the new server were still at 1.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app routes all SELECTs to 2 replicas and writes to the primary. After a release, support tickets say "I posted a comment, refreshed, and it vanished, then it came back". Primary: 1,500 writes/s. Replicas look healthy, CPU 40%. A quick check shows:

 application_name | state     | replay_lag
 replica1         | streaming | 00:00:00.004
 replica2         | streaming | 00:00:02.800

Replica2 runs nightly-style reports during the day too. The release added a "load comments" call fired immediately after POST. A red herring: the CDN also caches the comments API for 5 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and fix this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replication is slow, add more replicas" or "turn on synchronous replication everywhere". That ignores that lag is normal and the issue is routing and read-your-writes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the comment appear after a few seconds (lag, not data loss)? Do all users see it or mostly some (replica2)? Is the CDN cache in play (check cache headers)? Did the post-then-fetch pattern come with the release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route the follow-up read to the primary for a short window after a write (session flag or cookie, 5 s), and take replica2 out of the interactive pool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) read-after-write on a lagging replica, (b) replica2 lagged by report queries, (c) CDN caching, (d) lost write (unlikely since it reappears).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_replication on the primary for replay_lag per replica; pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on replicas; response headers (Age, Cache-Control) from the CDN; log which backend served the read.
  5. Root cause: Async replication plus a read issued milliseconds after the write; replica2 had ~2.8 s lag from long queries delaying replay.
  6. Fix: Short term: primary-read window after writes. Long term: LSN-aware routing:
-- after the write, on primary
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
-- before reading from a replica, on replica
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= '0/5A3F1C8'::pg_lsn;

Also an optimistic UI that shows the new comment locally, and a dedicated reporting replica. 7. Prevention: Alert on replay_lag > 1 s; separate interactive and reporting replicas; integration test that writes then reads through the router. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not send everything to the primary (kills the point of replicas) nor use remote_apply globally (commit latency for everyone).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Replica lag hits 60 s during a bulk job? -> Router falls back to primary based on lag threshold, throttle the batch.
  • User has two devices? -> The write-window flag must be keyed by user, stored server-side or carrying an LSN token.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a checkout page showed an empty cart after "Add" because the cart read hit a replica 3 s behind; an LSN token in the session cookie ended the tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network or adds replicas.
  • Hire: identifies read-after-write on async replicas and uses a primary-read window.
  • Strong hire: LSN-based routing, lag alerting, replica role separation, names the CDN as a red herring and verifies it.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java service moved behind PgBouncer to cut connections. After the rollout, intermittent errors appear: "prepared statement S_12 does not exist", jobs occasionally run twice, and a SET statement_timeout seems ignored. Config and code:

; pgbouncer.ini
[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 3000
default_pool_size = 30
// worker startup (runs once per connection)
stmt.execute("SET statement_timeout = '5s'");
// job lock
stmt.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42)");
doWork();
stmt.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42)");

Red herring: CPU on Postgres is at 30%, so "capacity" is not the problem.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase default_pool_size." The symptoms are about session state, not capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: PgBouncer and driver versions (protocol-level prepared statement support)? Does the app use JDBC server-side prepares? How many app instances?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Point the job runners at a session-mode pool or directly at Postgres while I fix the code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Transaction mode hands a different server connection each transaction, so (a) prepared statements created on one server connection are missing on the next, (b) the session-level SET applied to a connection another client now uses, (c) the advisory lock is held by a server connection that is returned to the pool and handed to another client, so two workers think they own or both unlock wrongly.
  4. How I'd verify each: SHOW POOLS;/SHOW SERVERS; in the PgBouncer console; pg_locks for advisory locks and their pids; JDBC logs of prepare/parse.
  5. Root cause: Using session-scoped features through a transaction-mode pooler.
  6. Fix: Use SET LOCAL inside the transaction, or set timeout per role/database; use pg_advisory_xact_lock within the transaction; disable server-side prepares (prepareThreshold=0) or use a PgBouncer version that supports protocol-level prepared statements (verify your version).
conn.setAutoCommit(false);
stmt.execute("SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s'");
stmt.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(42)");
doWork();
conn.commit(); // lock released automatically
  1. Prevention: Test suite against PgBouncer in transaction mode; lint for pg_advisory_lock, SET without LOCAL, LISTEN.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move everything to session mode (loses multiplexing); keep session mode only for the few components that need it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• LISTEN/NOTIFY needed? -> Needs a dedicated direct or session-mode connection.
  • Is the pooler a single point of failure? -> Yes, run several behind a load balancer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a nightly job's advisory lock leaked across pooled connections and blocked the next day's run until the connection was recycled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases pool size.
  • Hire: spots the three session-state features and fixes them.
  • Strong hire: also tests in CI against the pooler and plans pooler HA.

questions.promptHtml: Compare pg_dump and physical base backups. Which would you use for a 1 TB production database and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you can reason about restore time, not just backup creation, and know what PITR needs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: pg_dump is a logical, portable export that can restore one table or move across versions, but restore replays inserts and rebuilds indexes, so for 1 TB it takes many hours. A physical base backup copies the data files, restores about as fast as the copy, and with WAL archiving gives point-in-time recovery. For production I use physical (pgBackRest or similar) and keep pg_dump only for small targeted or cross-version needs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Logical Physical
Output SQL or custom dump Data files plus WAL
Restore Slow (indexes rebuilt) Fast
Cross-version Yes No
PITR No Yes
Granularity Table/schema Cluster 
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -f /backups/app appdb
pg_restore -j 4 -d appdb_restored /backups/app
pg_basebackup -D /backups/base -Ft -z -X stream -P

Copy speed example: 200 MB/s means 1 TB in about 1.5 hours; restore similar plus WAL replay. Storage snapshots are fast but check consistency guarantees with your provider. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media, one off-site and off-account; encrypt; and restore regularly in a drill.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never testing a restore.
  • Backups in the same account/disk as production.
  • Calling a replica a backup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is pg_restore slow? -> Index builds, constraint validation and per-row insert work dominate.
  2. How do you protect against ransomware? -> Immutable/object-lock storage in a separate account.
  3. What is your RTO for this database? -> Measured from a drill: restore plus replay plus validation plus cutover.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "pg_dump daily". Senior: states RTO from measured restores, uses WAL archive, isolates backups from the production blast radius.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A public 2017 postmortem showed five backup mechanisms, none restorable when needed; the lesson is restore tests.

questions.contextHtml: At 10:42 UTC an engineer ran DELETE FROM orders; on production (no WHERE). It was noticed at 10:50. The database is 1.2 TB, the app takes about 300 writes/s, WAL archiving to object storage with pgBackRest is on, last full backup was at 02:00, and the replica is already identical (it replayed the delete). Business wants orders back and as little downtime as possible. Another team suggests failing over to the replica.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fail over to the replica" (it has the delete) or "restore the last backup" and lose 8 hours of orders.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact time of the delete (from logs/log_statement or app audit)? Any other tables touched? Is WAL continuous since 02:00? How much downtime can we accept?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the offending path (revoke the credential, pause the job), keep prod running for other tables, and do not touch the replica's WAL archive. Optionally set the app to read-only for orders.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Only one: the data exists in the base backup plus WAL up to 10:41:59. The question is whether the archive is complete.
  4. How I'd verify: pgbackrest info, check archive range covers 10:41:59; test restore target on a separate host.
  5. Root cause: Unrestricted DML access to production with no guardrail.
  6. Fix: Restore the latest base backup onto a NEW server, replay WAL to just before the delete, then copy rows back.
restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-get %f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-09 10:41:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'

Use pause first, inspect SELECT count(*) FROM orders, then dump the missing rows (COPY ... TO) and insert them into production, preserving writes after 10:42. Expect roughly 1.5 to 3 hours (illustrative). 7. Prevention: Least-privilege roles, require transactions with row-count checks, delayed replica (recovery_min_apply_delay), regular restore drills, blocking DELETE without WHERE via tooling. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not swap the restored server in as prod unless the other tables also got damaged, because that discards 10:42 onward writes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• WAL archive has a gap at 06:00? -> Recovery can only reach the gap; fall back to the nearest valid time and reconcile from app logs.
  • Foreign keys cascade to order_items? -> Recover both tables from the same point.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team found in a drill that archive_command had been failing for days; the alert was missing, so they only had the base backup time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fails over to the replica or restores only the old backup.
  • Hire: base backup plus WAL replay to a point in time on a new server.
  • Strong hire: pauses to verify, copies rows instead of swapping, covers prevention and archive monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: A long report on a hot standby gets "canceling statement due to conflict with recovery". Why does that happen and what are your options?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests understanding of MVCC interacting with WAL replay, a classic replica pitfall.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The primary's VACUUM removes dead row versions and writes that to WAL. If the standby's query still needs those versions, replay would break its snapshot. Postgres either delays replay up to max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30 s) and then cancels the query. I can raise the delay on a dedicated reporting replica, or turn on hot_standby_feedback so the primary keeps rows, at the cost of bloat.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The standby has no control over what the primary vacuums. Replay is strictly ordered, so a conflicting record must either wait or kill the query.

Primary: VACUUM removes old tuple -> WAL
Standby: report snapshot needs that tuple
         replay waits <= max_standby_streaming_delay
         then: cancel query  (or lag grows if delay = -1)

Options:

  1. Dedicated reporting replica with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 and no user traffic; lag grows, accept it.
  2. hot_standby_feedback = on: standby reports its oldest snapshot so the primary holds back vacuum. Costs table bloat on the primary.
  3. Move reporting to a warehouse via CDC.
  4. Shorter queries, better indexes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling feedback on a replica with 6-hour queries and then wondering why the primary bloats.
  • Reading lag alerts without noticing replay is paused by a long query.
  • Using the same replica for interactive and reporting traffic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you see the cause? -> pg_stat_database_conflicts on the standby.
  2. What does feedback do to the primary? -> Delays row cleanup, so bloat grows like a long transaction.
  3. Which choice for a 40-minute nightly report? -> A dedicated replica with unbounded delay, or CDC to analytics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "increase the timeout". Senior: knows it is a vacuum/replay conflict, weighs feedback versus unbounded delay, and separates workloads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams turned on feedback for dashboards and later saw the primary's largest table double in size.

questions.contextHtml:
3 a.m. page: the primary's data volume is 96% full and growing at about 4 GB/h. Normal database growth is 1 GB/day. df shows the pg_wal directory at 380 GB (usually 4 GB).

 slot_name | active | restart_lsn | wal_status
 replica_old   | f  | 5/1A000000  | extended
 replica1      | t  | 8/F2000000  | reserved

Last week a team decommissioned a staging replica (replica_old) but nobody dropped its slot. Red herring: archive_command also shows a few failures from the same night.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deleting files from pg_wal by hand, which can corrupt the cluster.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is replica1 current? Any other inactive slots? Is archiving healthy? How much free space is left and at what rate does it fall?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the inactive slot (confirmed unused): SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('replica_old');. A checkpoint then lets old WAL be recycled. If space is nearly gone, add disk first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) inactive slot pinning WAL, (b) failing archive_command retaining segments, (c) a lagging active replica.
  4. How I'd verify each: the slots query above; pg_stat_archiver for failed_count; pg_stat_replication for lag.
  5. Root cause: A slot makes the primary retain WAL until the consumer confirms; the consumer was gone.
  6. Fix: Drop the slot; fix archiver; set max_slot_wal_keep_size = 100GB so a stuck slot is invalidated instead of filling the disk. Never delete files from pg_wal manually.
  7. Prevention: Alert on slot restart_lsn age and inactive slots; decommission runbook includes dropping slots; disk alert on pg_wal.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: max_slot_wal_keep_size can invalidate a slow replica, which then needs a re-bootstrap; I accept that to protect the primary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the slot belongs to a live but very slow replica? -> Fix the replica or let the cap invalidate it and rebuild with pg_basebackup.
  • Logical slot from Debezium stalled? -> Same risk, so alert on consumer lag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a CDC connector was paused for a weekend change freeze; its slot retained 700 GB and took the primary down on Monday.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes WAL files or restarts the database.
  • Hire: finds and drops the dead slot.
  • Strong hire: sets a cap, alerts on slots, and separates the archiver red herring.

questions.promptHtml: Design automatic failover for a Postgres primary with two standbys. What stops split brain?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The difference between a script and a safe HA system is consensus and fencing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I need five pieces: failure detection with a tolerant timeout, leader election in a consensus store like etcd so only one node can win, promotion of the best standby, client routing through HAProxy or a virtual IP, and fencing so the old primary cannot take writes. Patroni implements this: the leader holds a key with a TTL, and if it cannot renew, it demotes itself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Patroni node1 -> etcd leader key (TTL 30s)  <- node2, node3 compete
HAProxy health-checks "is primary" -> routes writes

Timeline: primary dies at T0; leader key expires after ttl (30 s); the most up-to-date standby takes the key, promotes (~1 s), HAProxy switches (~5 s). About 35 s of unavailability; with async replication you can lose recent commits. Choosing the candidate: highest replayed LSN, preferably the sync standby.

Split brain prevention layers: consensus (only one key holder), self-demotion when the lease cannot be renewed (watchdog), and STONITH/network fencing. The old primary rejoins with pg_rewind if it diverged.

Trade-off: shorter timeouts mean faster failover but more false positives from network blips.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Failover without fencing.
  • Claiming zero downtime.
  • Forgetting app reconnect and retry logic and DNS TTLs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does etcd run? -> Three or five nodes, separate from the database hosts' failure domain.
  2. What if etcd is down? -> Patroni demotes the primary to avoid split brain (unless configured otherwise), so etcd HA matters.
  3. How do you pick the new primary? -> Most advanced LSN, sync standby first, and no replica lag beyond a limit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "promote the replica". Senior: consensus, lease, fencing, pg_rewind, client routing, and quantified RTO/RPO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The classic bad night is a flaky network that causes promotion while the old primary is alive.

questions.contextHtml:
A self-managed cluster (primary A, standbys B and C, scripted failover with a VIP, no consensus store) had a 40-second network blip between the monitor and A. The script promoted B and moved the VIP. A kept running and still had 120 app connections pinned by IP. Over 11 minutes, A accepted 18,000 writes and B accepted 41,000. Detected when two customers saw different balances.

monitor: A unreachable x3 (30s) -> promote B
A: still accepting connections on 10.0.0.5
timelines diverged at LSN 4/9A000000

Red herring: the engineers first suspected data corruption on B.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review. What failed, how do you recover data, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout to 60 s." That reduces frequency but keeps the design flaw.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which clients reached which node? Do writes overlap on the same rows? Do we have WAL from the divergence point on both? Is money involved (priority)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fence A now: stop Postgres or block its port; send all traffic to B. Freeze both timelines for forensics.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lack of fencing, no quorum, detector watched only one network path.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare timelines (pg_controldata, timeline history files), diff the divergent rows.
  5. Root cause: Failure detection was not leader election; nothing prevented two primaries.
  6. Fix: Data: pick B as the truth; export A's 18,000 post-divergence writes (logical decoding or WAL inspection), reconcile with business rules and replay on B; then rebuild A as a standby using pg_rewind or fresh basebackup. System: Patroni with etcd, watchdog, HAProxy checking /primary, STONITH.
  7. Prevention: Chaos drills that partition the primary; alert on two nodes reporting pg_is_in_recovery() = false; application connection strings via a routed endpoint, not direct IPs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not auto-merge divergent writes without business review; quorum may reduce availability when a minority is isolated, which I accept.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Both sides wrote to the same account? -> Needs manual reconciliation from event logs; maybe ledger entries are append-only to simplify.
  • Why not synchronous replication alone? -> It limits data loss but does not stop two nodes from believing they are primary.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team set the failover timeout shorter after a past outage, then promoted during a routine switch maintenance; fencing later became a launch requirement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lengthens a timeout.
  • Hire: identifies split brain and the need for consensus and fencing.
  • Strong hire: includes reconciliation plan, pg_rewind, drills, and monitoring for dual primaries.

questions.contextHtml:
A 16-core, 64 GB Postgres runs behind 100 pods, each with a HikariCP pool of 20 (2,000 connections). max_connections = 2200. Every deploy, p99 jumps from 40 ms to 4 s for 3 minutes, and logs show:

FATAL: sorry, too many clients already
vmstat: r=180 cs=420000 us=55 sy=35
pg_stat_activity: 1,950 rows, 40 active, 1,900 idle

Traffic is about to grow 10x and the team proposes max_connections = 10000 and a bigger instance.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raise max_connections and RAM. That worsens context switching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Average active queries vs idle? Transaction length? Any session state needed (prepared statements, advisory locks, LISTEN)? App framework retry behaviour?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stagger pod restarts (maxSurge/rolling), shrink app pools to ~5 to 10 each.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) too many connections thrash scheduler (sy=35%, cs 420k), (b) startup storm exhausts max_connections, (c) per-connection memory from work_mem, (d) slow queries (unlikely: only 40 active).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_activity grouped by state; vmstat/pidstat -w; compare active count to cores (rule: 2 to 4 active per core, so about 32 to 64 here).
  5. Root cause: 2,000 mostly idle connections; the rolling deploy opens hundreds at once.
  6. Fix: PgBouncer in transaction mode:
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40
reserve_pool_size = 5

Fix session-state assumptions first, keep app pools small, and run PgBouncer in HA (two instances behind a load balancer). At 10x, add replicas for reads rather than connections. 7. Prevention: Alert on connections / max_connections > 70%; connection budget per service; startup jitter in pods. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set max_connections = 10000 (each backend is a process with memory); transaction mode costs some features, so I choose it deliberately.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Long transactions hold server connections? -> Pool exhausts; fix transaction scope, add query_wait_timeout and watch waiting clients.
  • RDS Proxy instead? -> Similar idea, managed; check its pinning behaviour with session state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team doubled the instance size and got no gain; a pooler dropping 2,000 connections to 40 cut p99 by 5x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises max_connections.
  • Hire: pooler plus smaller app pools.
  • Strong hire: sizes by cores, covers session-state hazards, pooler HA, and deploy jitter.

questions.contextHtml:
Postgres 12 (3 TB, 2,500 writes/s, 200 tables) must reach 16 with a cutover window under 60 seconds. Business forbids a 6-hour dump/restore. Known facts: 14 tables have no primary key, the app uses sequences heavily, there is a monthly ALTER TABLE migration, and the primary has 20% IO headroom. A trial subscription copied 2.1 TB but UPDATEs on a keyless table errored on the publisher.

ERROR: cannot update table "audit_log" because it does not have a replica identity and publishes updates

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set up logical replication and switch." No plan for keyless tables, sequences, DDL, validation or rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we add PKs? Are large objects used (not replicated)? Allowed freeze on DDL for the period? What's rollback tolerance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; protect the primary: throttle initial sync, check IO headroom, set max_slot_wal_keep_size.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: keyless tables, sequence drift, DDL drift, replication lag at cutover, extension differences.
  4. How I'd verify: Build the new cluster, load schema with pg_dump --schema-only, check row counts and checksums on samples, monitor pg_stat_subscription and slot lag.
  5. Root cause (of the error): UPDATE/DELETE need a replica identity.
  6. Fix: ALTER TABLE audit_log REPLICA IDENTITY FULL (or add a PK); freeze DDL; at cutover: stop writes (or read-only), wait for lag zero, copy sequence values (setval with a safety margin), switch the app endpoint, keep reverse logical replication from new to old for rollback.
ALTER TABLE audit_log REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
SELECT setval('orders_id_seq', (SELECT last_value FROM orders_id_seq) + 100000);
  1. Prevention: Rehearse twice in staging with production-sized data; a runbook with timings; app retry on reconnect.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Avoid pg_upgrade --link without a rollback path; FULL identity is heavy for large tables so prefer adding a PK.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lag never reaches zero? -> Find the slow table apply, parallelise by splitting publications, or schedule cutover at low traffic.
  • Large objects? -> Not replicated; migrate separately.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cutover succeeded but the first inserts failed on duplicate keys because sequences were left at their initial values.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ignores PKs and sequences.
  • Hire: handles replica identity, sequences, cutover.
  • Strong hire: reverse replication for rollback, rehearsals, DDL freeze, validation.

questions.contextHtml: Current setup: nightly pg_dump of a 1.5 TB database to a bucket in the same cloud account, taking 7 hours and using 1 TB of storage per copy at 30 copies retained (cost about 30 TB). Last quarter's untested restore attempt ran for 19 hours. The new RPO target is 5 minutes, RTO 2 hours. Budget is flat. An engineer proposes "just add a replica, it is a backup".
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the backup approach and justify the cost.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a replica" or "dump more often". Neither meets RPO or RTO.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Compliance retention? Per-table restores needed? Cross-region requirement? Who can delete the bucket?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do a restore drill this week of the current backup to know the real RTO; add a second copy in another account.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The design fails RPO (24 h), RTO (19 h), and the blast radius (same account).
  4. How I'd verify: Time a physical restore in staging; check WAL volume per hour to size archive.
  5. Root cause: Logical dumps optimise portability, not recovery speed.
  6. Fix: pgBackRest: weekly full, daily differential/incremental, continuous WAL archive for 5-minute (or better) RPO, compression plus encryption, repository in a separate account with object lock. Retain 14 days PITR plus monthly fulls; keep occasional pg_dump for cross-version or table-level needs. Incremental/differential cuts storage to maybe a third (verify with your data), offsetting the added WAL storage. Estimated RTO from a drill: restore around 1 to 1.5 hours at 300 MB/s plus WAL replay.
  7. Prevention: Automated monthly restore test with row-count and checksum validation; alerts on archive lag, failed archive_command, repository age.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A replica gives HA, not history; I keep both. Longer retention costs more; I pick it from compliance and the time to detect mistakes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need RPO 0? -> Sync standby plus archive, accepting commit latency.
  • Restore one table from 3 days ago? -> Restore PITR to a scratch server and extract it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team's nightly dump silently produced empty files after a permissions change; only a scheduled restore test found it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: replica as backup.
  • Hire: physical backups plus WAL archive meeting RPO/RTO.
  • Strong hire: separate-account immutable storage, automated restore tests, costed trade-offs.
